content: The Prior Informed Consent (PIC) procedure was incorporated into the London Guidelines in 1989. Its primary objectives were to assist importing countries in understanding the potential hazards of chemicals being shipped to them, establish a decision-making process for future imports, and encourage exporting countries to prevent the export of unwanted pesticides. In 1998, the PIC procedure became legally binding under the Rotterdam Convention on the Prior Informed Consent Procedure for Certain Hazardous Chemicals and Pesticides in International Trade. This Convention, which came into effect in 2004, applies to both pesticides and industrial chemicals. While it includes some obligations related to domestic production and use, its main focus is on regulating the import and export of chemicals. The PIC procedure serves as a formal mechanism for obtaining and sharing decisions made by importing countries regarding hazardous chemicals. Chemicals listed in Annex III of the Convention can only be exported in accordance with the importing country’s decision, aiming to protect human health and the environment by facilitating informed decisions about the trade of hazardous substances. Once a chemical is listed in Annex III, all parties to the Rotterdam Convention are required to implement the PIC procedure for that chemical. The Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs), which also came into force in 2004, aims to eliminate the production and use of chemicals classified as POPs. These are organic compounds that persist in the environment, accumulate in the fatty tissues of living organisms, and are toxic to humans and wildlife. POPs are particularly dangerous due to their long-term effects, even though these may not be immediately apparent. The Convention categorizes chemicals into three lists: Annex A for chemicals to be eliminated, Annex B for those to be restricted, and Annex C for unintentional by-products of certain production processes that need to be reduced. Parties to the Convention are obligated to prohibit the production and use of most chemicals listed in Annexes A and B at the national level, with specific exemptions for certain uses, such as disease vector control. The Convention also includes provisions for the environmentally sound disposal of POP stockpiles and waste. The Basel Convention on the Transboundary Movement of Hazardous Wastes and Their Disposal, effective since 1992, regulates the international shipment of hazardous wastes, including obsolete pesticides and by-products from pesticide production. This Convention is particularly valuable for countries seeking to prevent the dumping of hazardous waste within their borders, especially when they lack the capacity to manage such waste in an environmentally sound manner. It requires exporting states to notify importing states in writing and obtain their consent before moving hazardous wastes across borders. The Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer addresses the use of methyl bromide, a pesticide that harms the ozone layer. Industrialized countries were required to eliminate its production by January 2005, with exceptions for pre-shipment, quarantine, and critical uses where alternatives were not immediately available. Developing countries were granted a grace period but have agreed to phase out methyl bromide on an accelerated timeline. Several International Labour Organization (ILO) conventions address the safety and health of workers exposed to chemicals, including pesticides. The most relevant is the Safety and Health in Agriculture Convention (C184), adopted in 2001 and effective in 2003, which imposes responsibilities on employers, strengthens workers' rights, and requires governments to develop national policies on agricultural safety and health. However, many agricultural workers, particularly informal laborers, are not covered by occupational health and safety legislation. The ILO Convention No. 182 on the Worst Forms of Child Labour, adopted in 1999, identifies work that harms the health, safety, or morals of children as a worst form of child labor, which includes pesticide application due to children’s increased vulnerability to toxic effects. The Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC) aims to eliminate chemical weapons by prohibiting their development, production, stockpiling, and use. Some pesticides are chemically related to compounds listed under the CWC, which may have implications for their production, importation, and storage. Non-binding international instruments, such as the Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management, provide guidance on pesticide management throughout their lifecycle. Originally adopted in 1985 and revised in 2013, the Code serves as a reference framework for governments, the pesticide industry, and other stakeholders. It is supported by technical guidelines that offer detailed advice on specific aspects of pesticide management, such as registration, labeling, and data requirements. Although voluntary, the Code has significantly influenced national pesticide legislation. The Codex Alimentarius Commission (CAC), a joint body of the FAO and WHO, establishes harmonized food standards, including maximum residue limits (MRLs) for pesticides. The Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS) is an international tool for chemical hazard communication, covering all chemicals, including pesticides. It provides standardized criteria for hazard classification and labeling, replacing the WHO Classification of Pesticides by Hazard. GHS includes chronic human toxicity and environmental toxicity in addition to acute human toxicity, making it more comprehensive. Many countries are adopting GHS as a binding standard through national legislation. Countries can meet their international legal obligations through various approaches, such as incorporating treaty obligations directly into national law, transposing international requirements into national legislation, or adjusting national laws to align with international instruments. Regional collaboration in pesticide regulation, such as harmonized registration procedures and mutual recognition agreements, can facilitate trade, share resources, and improve pesticide management. Examples include the European Union’s Regulation (EC) No. 1107/2009, which sets approval criteria for active substances, and the Sahelian Pesticide Committee, which centralizes pesticide registration for nine member states in West Africa. Regional collaboration may require adjustments to national legislation to recognize regional authorities or harmonized standards. National pesticide legislation must be tailored to the country’s legal framework and circumstances, considering factors such as constitutional provisions, division of powers in federal systems, and individual rights to health, a clean environment, and adequate food and water.
